title: AI and regulation are reshaping the future of building security
excerpt: Regulation can reinforce security both physically and digitally.
content_html:
Criminals used to rely on lock-picking tools and crowbars to break into buildings. Today’s attackers can cause just as much damage and disruption by using phishing links, malware and sophisticated digital exploits to target products, systems and networks.

The truth is, today’s security challenge isn’t just physical – or cyber – but both. And keeping one step ahead of criminals is a full-time occupation. For those people tasked with researching and developing the latest products, it sometimes means using unconventional tactics, such as using professional lock pickers to test the security and resilience of new products.

SVP & Chief Technology Officer for EMEIA at ASSA ABLOY Opening Solutions.

While modern locks are still based on mechanical engineering, they are more advanced than they look. Improvements in design, materials, and manufacturing mean they are stronger, more reliable, and harder to tamper with. But there’s more to locks than just security.

Some systems can even use the motion of turning a key to generate a small amount of electrical energy, which provides energy to power extra functions without wiring or batteries. This means they are not just standalone locks but can also be used as part of wider digital access systems.

Used extensively in buildings such as offices, hotels, hospitals and other critical infrastructure, these modern digital access solutions can also connect to cloud-based platforms to manage who can enter buildings and restricted areas.

Bridging physical and digital security

However, digital systems have their own security risks, which means security teams need to anticipate and defend against a wide range of risks – from attempts to breach access platforms to phishing attacks – as well as other tactics designed to exploit human behavior.

This explains why some security personnel have to adopt a ‘hacker’s mindset’ to keep systems safe. And that means continuously testing, probing, and strengthening systems to identify vulnerabilities.

But what is becoming increasingly clear is that physical and digital security systems can no longer be treated as separate entities.

Many security solutions today employ both mechanical and digital technology, which means that resilience – the kind of resilience that keeps data centers safe, for example – depends on understanding how risks move across systems, people and environments.

Embedding resilience into design

That means continuously designing and testing products against existing real-world threats while also anticipating what might be around the corner. That includes building security into every stage of development, especially as technology evolves.

For instance, great strides have been made recently in terms of biometric authentication, including facial recognition and fingerprint scanning. Similarly, smartphones are increasingly being used to secure credentials for mobile-based access control systems.

Work is also currently underway to use artificial intelligence (AI) to analyze data in real time to identify unusual entry times, identify multiple failed authentication attempts, or spot any other anomalies that might suggest someone is trying to gain entry illegally.

Using AI tools in a positive way is important because it is also the source of some of the newest and, therefore, most unpredictable challenges. For example, there are now autonomous AI threat chains that can discover and exploit vulnerabilities unilaterally, moving from reconnaissance to exfiltration in record time without any need for human oversight.

The danger posed by cyber criminals has also become more complex due to the growing interconnectivity of digital products and services. In many ways, a world where all hardware and software are interconnected is an efficient and convenient one.

But it is also one where, if bad actors gain access to a single element, they may be able to compromise the whole network.

The importance of regulation and compliance

This is something that the European Union (EU) is actively addressing. For instance, the European Union’s (EU) NIS2 Directive relates to cybersecurity protecting network and information systems and significantly broadens both the scope and the obligations for compliance.

It also takes an “all-hazard” approach to security, which means protecting not just digital networks and systems, but also the physical environments in which they operate.

Similarly, the EU’s Cyber Resilience Act is designed to ensure that all digital products are safe from cyber threats.

Its goal is to ensure that connected devices and software are built, updated, and maintained with security in mind, helping protect users in an increasingly connected world.

And by introducing clearer requirements and standards, the CRA will help consumers and organizations identify products with strong security features and configure them more securely from the outset.

In both cases, not only is it incumbent on vendors to meet or exceed these rules and regulations, but also to keep customers, the wider industry, and other stakeholders informed about developments.

Not only must businesses contend with the usual challenges from phishing and malware, but the rapid growth of AI has introduced a new and unpredictable dimension to keeping out online criminals. Security – both physical and cyber – has never been more critical than it is today.

虽然现代锁仍然基于机械工程，但它们比看起来更先进。 设计、材料和制造方面的改进意味着它们更坚固、更可靠、更难以篡改。 但锁的意义不仅仅在于安全。

有些系统甚至可以利用转动钥匙的动作来产生少量电能，从而无需接线或电池即可为额外功能提供能量。 这意味着它们不仅仅是独立的锁，还可以用作更广泛的数字访问系统的一部分。

这些现代数字访问解决方案广泛应用于办公室、酒店、医院和其他关键基础设施等建筑物，还可以连接到基于云的平台来管理谁可以进入建筑物和限制区域。

连接物理和数字安全

然而，数字系统有其自身的安全风险，这意味着安全团队需要预测和防御各种风险（从尝试破坏访问平台到网络钓鱼攻击）以及旨在利用人类行为的其他策略。

这解释了为什么一些安全人员必须采用“黑客思维”来保证系统安全。 这意味着不断测试、探索和强化系统以识别漏洞。

但越来越清楚的是，物理和数字安全系统不能再被视为独立的实体。

如今，许多安全解决方案都采用机械和数字技术，这意味着弹性（例如，保持数据中心安全的弹性）取决于对风险如何在系统、人员和环境之间转移的了解。

将弹性融入设计

这意味着针对现有的现实威胁不断设计和测试产品，同时预测即将发生的情况。 这包括将安全性融入到开发的每个阶段，尤其是随着技术的发展。

例如，最近在生物识别认证方面取得了巨大进步，包括面部识别和指纹扫描。 同样，智能手机越来越多地用于保护基于移动的访问控制系统的凭证。

目前正在开展使用人工智能 (AI) 实时分析数据的工作，以识别异常进入时间、识别多次失败的身份验证尝试，或发现可能表明有人试图非法进入的任何其他异常情况。

以积极的方式使用人工智能工具非常重要，因为它也是一些最新的、因此也是最不可预测的挑战的根源。 例如，现在有自主的人工智能威胁链，可以单方面发现和利用漏洞，在创纪录的时间内从侦察到渗透，无需人工监督。

由于数字产品和服务的互联性不断增强，网络犯罪分子带来的危险也变得更加复杂。 从很多方面来说，所有硬件和软件互连的世界都是一个高效且便捷的世界。

但这也是一种情况，如果不良行为者获得对单个元素的访问权限，他们可能能够危害整个网络。

监管和合规的重要性

这是欧盟（EU）正在积极解决的问题。 例如，欧盟 (EU) NIS2 指令涉及保护网络和信息系统的网络安全，并显着扩大了合规范围和义务。

它还采取“万无一失”的安全方法，这意味着不仅保护数字网络和系统，还保护它们运行的​​物理环境。

同样，欧盟的网络弹性法案旨在确保所有数字产品免受网络威胁。

其目标是确保互联设备和软件的构建、更新和维护都考虑到安全性，从而帮助在日益互联的世界中保护用户。

通过引入更明确的要求和标准，CRA 将帮助消费者和组织识别具有强大安全功能的产品，并从一开始就更安全地配置它们。

在这两种情况下，供应商不仅有责任满足或超越这些规则和规定，而且有责任让客户、更广泛的行业和其他利益相关者了解进展情况。

企业不仅必须应对网络钓鱼和恶意软件带来的常见挑战，而且人工智能的快速发展也为防范网络犯罪引入了新的、不可预测的维度。 物理安全和网络安全从未像现在这样重要。
